sentimental

/sen-tuh-MEN-tul/ — stress on third syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sentimental describes feelings, memories, or objects that stir up tenderness, nostalgia, or emotional attachment.

He kept the broken watch for sentimental reasons — it had belonged to his grandfather.

Worked Example

An elderly woman opens a box of letters written by her late husband during their courtship, and even though decades have passed, she reads through them with tears and a soft smile.

The word 'sentimental' captures not just that the letters matter to her, but that their value lies entirely in the emotions and tender memories they stir. Their worth is emotional and memory-bound, not monetary or practical. A plainer word like 'meaningful' wouldn't convey that specific emotional attachment to the past.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tender: Tender means gentle, soft, and warmly affectionate — a tender hug, a tender tone with a crying child. It describes how you treat someone in the moment. Sentimental describes why an object or memory matters: it is loaded with feelings about the past. A nurse can be tender with a stranger; only a keepsake's owner is sentimental about it.

touching: Touching describes something that stirs warm emotion in the people watching or reading — a touching reunion moves its audience. Sentimental points the other way: it is about the private attachment someone feels to their own memories and keepsakes. A stranger finds the story touching; the woman who lived it is sentimental about it.

wistful: Wistful is a quiet, dreamy sadness — gazing out the window, wishing for something out of reach. Sentimental is warmer and more attached: it treasures the object or memory it holds onto. A wistful mood drifts; sentimental feeling fastens onto a photograph, a song, an old postcard.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

detached: keeping feelings at a cool distance

dispassionate: ruled by calm reason, not feeling

Where it sits · how much tender feeling drives someone — practical → emotional → affectionate → sentimental

practical vs. sentimental: Practical sits at the opposite end of the scale from sentimental — a practical person values things for their usefulness, not for the tender memories a sentimental person treasures.

emotional vs. sentimental: Emotional is broader and weaker than sentimental; emotional covers any strong feeling, while sentimental points specifically to tenderness about memories, keepsakes, and the past.

affectionate vs. sentimental: Affectionate is close to sentimental but weaker here — affectionate shows warm feelings toward people, while sentimental pours those feelings into memories, objects, and everything they stand for.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — senti-

Root — senti-: to feel (from Latin sentire; the -i- links the root to the suffix)

Suffix — -ment

Suffix — -ment: forms nouns: the result or product of an action (Latin)

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: relating to, characterized by (adjective-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Senti- ('to feel', from Latin sentire) plus -ment builds sentiment, 'a feeling' — and adding -al makes sentimental: relating to, or driven by, tender feelings and emotional attachment.

Use the root in a new word: sentient

Use the root in a new word: sentient: Scientists debate whether robots could ever be sentient — able to feel — using the very root, sentire, that makes sentimental all about feelings.

Word Choice

neutral / everyday

Sentimental describes the emotional pull of objects or memories tied to the past. Use it when someone values something because of what it feels like to remember, not for practical use. In everyday speech, you might just say 'meaningful' or 'emotional,' but 'sentimental' is more precise about that memory-based, heart-tugging attachment.
